subject: biology

items.q: What is meant by the ecological niche of a species?
items.correct: The role of the species in its ecosystem, including its biotic and abiotic interactions
items.misconception: The place where the species lives, described by its location and ecosystem type
items.why: In everyday English a niche is a recess or a small sheltered space, and nature documentaries speak of animals 'finding a niche' in a landscape, so students read the word as a location. The habitat is also the first ecological term they meet, and every new term tends to be assimilated to it. The habitat is the place in which a species lives; the niche is what the species does there. A niche is described by interactions, such as what the species eats, what eats it, what it competes with and which abiotic conditions it tolerates, not by a location.
items.specStatementText: Niche is a role, not a place
items.random_wrong: The position of the species in a food chain, defined by the food it eats

items.q: Koalas (Phascolarctos cinereus) feed on Eucalyptus leaves, are active mainly at night, and are found in eucalypt woodland in eastern Australia where rainfall and temperature stay within particular ranges. Which statement about the ecological niche of the koala is correct?
items.correct: Its niche includes its Eucalyptus diet and its tolerance of rainfall and temperature
items.misconception: Its niche is fully described by its position as a primary consumer of leaves
items.why: Food chains and food webs dominate GCSE and MYP ecology, so students are used to characterising a species by its trophic position. Textbook examples of niche also usually lead with diet, so the other components are easily dropped. The guidance specifies that a niche includes the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence growth, survival and reproduction, of which how the species obtains food is only one. Two species that eat the same food but tolerate different temperatures, or are eaten by different predators, have different niches.
items.specStatementText: Niche is a role, not a place
items.random_wrong: Its niche is the eucalypt woodland of eastern Australia in which it lives and feeds

items.q: Which statement describes an obligate anaerobe?
items.correct: An organism that can grow only where oxygen gas is absent from its environment
items.misconception: An organism that does not use oxygen but is unharmed when oxygen gas is present
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is defined at GCSE simply as respiration without oxygen, so students picture anaerobes as organisms that ignore oxygen. Nothing in their earlier courses suggests that oxygen can be harmful to a living cell. The distinguishing feature of an obligate anaerobe is that it cannot tolerate oxygen gas in its environment; oxygen kills it or prevents its growth, which is why such organisms are found in oxygen-free places such as deep sediments, waterlogged soil and the gut.
items.random_wrong: An organism that normally respires anaerobically but can use oxygen if needed

items.q: Three bacteria were cultured in liquid medium. Bacterium X grew only in a tube open to the air. Bacterium Y grew in both an open tube and a sealed oxygen-free tube, forming a denser culture in the open tube. Bacterium Z grew only in the sealed oxygen-free tube. Which classification is correct?
items.correct: X obligate aerobe; Y facultative anaerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, by oxygen tolerance
items.misconception: X obligate aerobe; Y obligate aerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, as Y grew better with oxygen
items.why: Students read 'obligate' as 'preferred' rather than 'required', and compare the amount of growth in the two conditions rather than asking whether growth is possible in each. The classification depends on tolerance, not on which condition gives more growth. The question to ask is whether the organism can grow at all with oxygen absent and with oxygen present. Growth in both means facultative anaerobe; growth only with oxygen means obligate aerobe.
items.random_wrong: X obligate aerobe; Y obligate anaerobe; Z obligate anaerobe, as Y can grow without oxygen

items.q: In which groups of organisms is photosynthesis the mode of nutrition?
items.correct: Plants, algae and several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria
items.misconception: Plants and algae only, because prokaryotes are unable to photosynthesize
items.why: GCSE teaches photosynthesis as the way 'plants make food', and bacteria are met mainly as pathogens or decomposers, so the existence of photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria is a surprise. Algae are often loosely called 'plants' in everyday speech. Photosynthesis is the mode of nutrition of plants, of algae (which are not plants) and of several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes. The details of the different types of prokaryotic photosynthesis are not required.
items.specStatementText: Photosynthesis feeds plants, algae and some prokaryotes
items.random_wrong: Plants, algae and any prokaryotes whose cells happen to contain chloroplasts

items.q: A dog eats meat. Proteins in the meat are hydrolysed in the gut, the amino acids pass across the wall of the small intestine into the blood, and later some of them are used in the dog's muscle cells to make new protein. Which term describes the use of the amino acids to make the dog's own protein?
items.correct: Assimilation, because the products of digestion become part of the dog
items.misconception: Absorption, because the amino acids are being taken into the dog's tissues
items.why: GCSE treatments of digestion end at absorption into the blood, so assimilation is a new term that students map onto the stage they already know. Both words begin with 'a' and both mean 'take in' in everyday speech. Holozoic nutrition has four stages: ingestion, digestion, absorption and assimilation. Assimilation comes after absorption: amino acids that have been absorbed into the blood are assimilated only when a cell uses them to make its own proteins.
items.random_wrong: Digestion, because it is the last step in the processing of the meat

items.q: Which statement about nutrition in animals is correct?
items.correct: Animals are heterotrophs that ingest, digest, absorb and assimilate food
items.misconception: Animals that host photosynthetic algae inside their cells are autotrophic
items.why: Popular accounts describe corals and some sea slugs as 'solar-powered' animals, and students locate the mode of nutrition in the body rather than in the organism whose cells carry out photosynthesis. The guidance states that all animals are heterotrophic. Photosynthesis in a coral is carried out by the algal cells, which are separate organisms; the coral animal obtains carbon compounds from the algae and by ingesting plankton, so its own mode of nutrition is heterotrophic.
items.random_wrong: Animals assimilate their food by absorbing it across the lining of the gut

items.q: Euglena gracilis is a freshwater protist with chloroplasts. Cultures grow in the light in a medium with no organic carbon compounds, and also grow in the dark when organic carbon compounds are supplied. Which statement about the nutrition of Euglena is correct?
items.correct: It is a facultative mixotroph, because either mode alone can sustain it
items.misconception: It is an autotroph, because an organism with chloroplasts cannot also be a heterotroph
items.why: Food chains present producers and consumers as mutually exclusive boxes, and the plant/animal dichotomy of early biology reinforces the idea that photosynthesis and feeding never occur in the same organism. Some protists are mixotrophic: they photosynthesize and also ingest or absorb carbon compounds from other organisms. Euglena is a freshwater example, and many mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton.
items.random_wrong: It is an obligate mixotroph, because it must photosynthesize whenever light is available

items.q: Which statement describes saprotrophic nutrition?
items.correct: Secretion of enzymes onto dead organic matter, followed by absorption of the products of digestion
items.misconception: Ingestion of dead organic matter, followed by internal digestion and absorption of products
items.why: Holozoic nutrition is the model of digestion students know, so they assume all heterotrophs ingest first and digest afterwards. The fungal body has no mouth or gut, but this is rarely made explicit. Saprotrophic nutrition is external digestion: enzymes are secreted onto the dead organic matter, and the products are absorbed by the fungus or bacterium. Nothing is ingested; digestion happens outside the organism.
items.random_wrong: Any feeding on dead organic matter, whether by fungi and bacteria or by earthworms and woodlice

items.q: Three species of archaea were studied. Species 1 obtains energy by oxidizing ammonia. Species 2 obtains energy by oxidizing carbon compounds absorbed from decaying matter. Species 3 obtains energy from light. What do these observations illustrate?
items.correct: Archaea are metabolically diverse, using light, inorganic chemicals or carbon compounds
items.misconception: Archaea are a group of bacteria, so they show the same modes of nutrition as other bacteria
items.why: The older name 'archaebacteria' persists in some textbooks, and archaea look like bacteria under a microscope, so students treat them as a subgroup of bacteria rather than a separate domain. The three-domain system places Archaea alongside Bacteria and Eukaryota. Being prokaryotic is a cell type, not a domain; archaea differ from bacteria in many fundamental ways and are metabolically very diverse.
items.specStatementText: Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse
items.random_wrong: Archaea are chemosynthetic extremophiles, so only species 1 is a typical archaeon

items.q: A skull of Paranthropus robustus, an extinct hominid, has very large flat molars with thick enamel, small incisors and canines, a massive lower jaw, and a sagittal crest along the top of the skull where large chewing muscles were attached. What can be deduced about its diet?
items.correct: A diet of tough plant material, since the teeth and jaw are adapted for prolonged grinding
items.misconception: A diet of meat, since large jaw muscles indicate a powerful bite for seizing and killing prey
items.why: Students' mental image of a powerful jaw comes from predators such as lions and crocodiles, so robustness of the skull is read as evidence of killing and meat-eating rather than of grinding. Meat is torn and sheared, which needs sharp cutting teeth, not prolonged chewing. Tough, fibrous plant food needs heavy grinding, so herbivores have large flat molars with thick enamel and the large jaw muscles, heavy jaws and crests that go with them.
items.random_wrong: An omnivorous diet, since the presence of canines shows that some meat was eaten

items.q: How were biologists able to deduce the diets of extinct hominids such as Paranthropus robustus?
items.correct: By applying theories relating dentition to diet, developed from observing living mammals, to the fossil teeth
items.misconception: By developing theories relating dentition to diet from the fossils themselves, then confirming them with living mammals
items.why: Fossils are the context in which students meet the idea, so they assume the fossils were the evidence for the theory rather than the cases to which it was applied. The NOS point is the direction of reasoning: observation of living mammals led to theories relating dentition to diet, and these theories then allowed the diets of extinct organisms to be deduced. The fossils could not have supplied the theory, because their owners' diets were not observable.
items.random_wrong: By comparing the size of the fossil jaws with those of living carnivores, since powerful jaws indicate meat-eating

items.q: An aphid feeds on a leaf without removing any tissue, whereas a caterpillar leaves ragged holes in the leaf. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: The aphid has piercing mouthparts that reach the sap, whereas the caterpillar has chewing mouthparts that bite off leaf tissue
items.misconception: Both insects have chewing mouthparts, but the aphid is so small that the holes it bites are too tiny to be seen
items.why: The chewed, holed leaf is the visible image of insect damage, and students have not looked at an aphid's stylet, so all insect feeding is assumed to be chewing. The guidance names two types of mouthpart. Chewing mouthparts remove and grind leaf tissue, while piercing mouthparts are fine stylets that enter the leaf without removing tissue and draw out sap.
items.random_wrong: The aphid pierces the leaf to inject a toxin that digests the tissue, whereas the caterpillar chews the tissue

items.q: Koalas feed almost entirely on Eucalyptus leaves, which contain high concentrations of terpenes, secondary compounds produced by the plant. Which statement best explains how koalas survive on this diet?
items.correct: Koalas have a metabolic adaptation: liver enzymes break the terpenes down for excretion
items.misconception: Koalas have become immune to the terpenes, which no longer have any effect on their cells
items.why: The everyday idea of 'immunity' or 'getting used to' something is applied, and students have not considered that a molecule entering the body must be dealt with chemically. The guidance refers to metabolic adaptations for detoxifying plant toxins. The toxin is chemically altered by the animal's enzymes, which is a specific adaptation of that species, not a general immunity.
items.random_wrong: The terpenes are waste the leaf cannot excrete, so they have no real effect on animals

items.q: Which statement correctly classifies an adaptation as chemical, physical or behavioural, and as belonging to a predator or a prey animal?
items.correct: A skunk spraying a foul-smelling secretion at an attacker is a chemical adaptation of a prey animal
items.misconception: A rattlesnake's venom is a physical adaptation of a predator, because it is injected through the fangs
items.why: Students classify adaptations by what they can see, and the fangs are visible while the venom is not, so the whole system is filed under the structure. The guidance distinguishes chemical, physical and behavioural adaptations. Venom, foul-smelling secretions and skin poisons are chemical adaptations; teeth, claws, shells and camouflage colouring are physical; hunting in groups or freezing are behavioural.
items.random_wrong: Zebras living in herds is not an adaptation, because this behaviour is learned rather than inherited

items.q: Which pairing of a rainforest plant with its strategy for harvesting light is correct?
items.correct: Strangler epiphyte: germinates high on a branch and later sends roots down to the soil
items.misconception: Liana: germinates on a high branch and grows roots down the trunk until they reach the soil
items.why: Mature strangler figs have a lattice of root stems reaching the ground and look like climbers, and both lianas and stranglers are shown wrapped around tree trunks in documentaries. A liana is rooted in the soil and climbs upwards. A strangler epiphyte does the opposite: it starts high on a branch, grows roots downwards, and may eventually kill the host tree as the roots fuse around the trunk and its crown shades the host.
items.specStatementText: Ways to reach the light in a forest
items.random_wrong: Epiphyte: absorbs water and carbon compounds from the xylem and phloem of the tree it grows on

items.q: Shrubs and herbs grow on the floor of a forest beneath a closed canopy. How do these plants obtain enough light to survive?
items.correct: They are shade tolerant, able to photosynthesize at the low light intensities reaching the floor
items.misconception: They obtain carbon compounds from the decaying leaf litter, so they need little light
items.why: 'Plants need sunlight' is a rule learned early, and the forest floor is visibly dark and littered with fungi, so students look for a fungus-like solution. Shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs growing on the forest floor are one of the plant strategies for harvesting light named in the guidance. They photosynthesize at low light intensities rather than needing to reach the canopy.
items.specStatementText: Ways to reach the light in a forest
items.random_wrong: They receive sugar from the canopy trees through underground fungal networks

items.q: On a rocky shore, adult barnacles of one species (Chthamalus) are found only high on the shore, while a second species (Balanus) occupies the middle and lower shore. When Balanus was removed from areas of the middle and lower shore, Chthamalus settled, survived and grew there. What do these results show?
items.correct: The fundamental niche of Chthamalus includes the lower shore, but competition restricts its realized niche
items.misconception: Chthamalus is absent from the lower shore because the physical conditions there are beyond its tolerance limits
items.why: Distribution is first explained through abiotic factors alone, and competition is invisible in a survey of where organisms are found, so the absence is attributed to the conditions. The realized niche is set by competition as well as by tolerance limits. Removal experiments, in which a competitor is taken away and the species spreads into the vacated area, show that the missing area was within the fundamental niche all along.
items.random_wrong: The realized niche of Chthamalus is the whole shore and its fundamental niche is the upper shore

items.q: Two species of Paramecium, P. aurelia and P. caudatum, both feed on bacteria. Grown in separate cultures with the same food supply, each species reached a stable population. Grown together in one culture, P. aurelia reached a similar density to when alone, while the population of P. caudatum declined steadily until almost none remained. Which conclusion is supported?
items.correct: P. caudatum was excluded from the culture because the two species occupied exactly the same niche
items.misconception: The two species would have reached a stable balance, sharing the bacteria, if the culture had been continued
items.why: Students picture nature as balanced and cooperative, and coexisting species that look similar are common, so they do not see that coexistence requires the niches to differ. Competitive exclusion means that no two species can occupy the same niche in the same place indefinitely. Species that coexist do so because their realized niches differ; each species has a niche unique to it.
items.random_wrong: P. aurelia eliminated P. caudatum by feeding on it, which is why the P. aurelia population stayed high

items.q: The fundamental niches of two species overlap and the two species compete. What are the possible outcomes?
items.correct: One species is eliminated, or both are restricted to part of their fundamental niche
items.misconception: The species that loses is driven to extinction throughout its range, wherever it occurs
items.why: 'Elimination' and 'exclusion' sound total, and laboratory examples such as Gause's Paramecium cultures end with one species at zero in the culture vessel, which students generalise to the whole species. The guidance gives two outcomes: elimination of one species from the area of competition, or restriction of both to a part of their fundamental niche. Neither is extinction of the species as a whole.
items.random_wrong: Both species continue to occupy their whole fundamental niches, sharing the resources between them

items.q: Two hominid skulls are compared. Skull A has very large flat molars with thick enamel, small canines, a massive lower jaw and a sagittal crest for large chewing muscles. Skull B has relatively small molars, small canines little larger than the incisors, a lighter jaw and no sagittal crest. What can be deduced about the diets of the two species?
items.correct: A was herbivorous, grinding tough plant material; B was omnivorous, with unspecialised teeth suited to a mixed diet
items.misconception: Both were carnivorous, because both skulls have canine teeth, which are the teeth used for tearing meat
items.why: Canines are labelled as 'for tearing meat' in school diagrams of dentition, and the word calls to mind dogs, so students take their mere presence as a diagnostic of carnivory. Dentition has to be read as a whole. The small canines, relatively small molars and unspecialised teeth of Homo sapiens indicate an omnivorous diet, not a carnivorous one; large flat molars and a heavy jaw indicate herbivory.
items.random_wrong: A was carnivorous, because a massive jaw and crest indicate a powerful killing bite; B was herbivorous

items.q: Are abiotic factors, such as temperature tolerance, part of a species' niche?
items.correct: Yes. The niche includes abiotic interactions, such as the ranges of temperature, water availability, pH and oxygen that the species can tolerate, as well as its biotic interactions.
items.misconception: A niche is made up only of interactions with other organisms; abiotic conditions belong to the description of the habitat instead.
items.why: Students are taught to separate biotic from abiotic factors, and because the habitat is a physical place they file all the physical conditions under 'habitat' and all the living interactions under 'niche'. The guidance defines the niche as including both biotic and abiotic interactions. The range of abiotic conditions a species tolerates is part of its role in the ecosystem, and it is what sets the tolerance limits of the fundamental niche.
items.specStatementText: Niche is a role, not a place
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every organism that can grow without oxygen an obligate anaerobe?
items.correct: No. Facultative anaerobes can also grow without oxygen; an obligate anaerobe is one that can grow only in the absence of oxygen because oxygen is toxic to it.
items.misconception: 'Anaerobe' and 'obligate anaerobe' mean the same thing: any organism able to respire without oxygen is an obligate anaerobe.
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses teach anaerobic respiration as a process without introducing categories of organism, so students meet the word 'anaerobe' without the distinction between 'can' and 'must'. The word 'obligate' is unfamiliar and is treated as decoration. The categories are defined by tolerance. An obligate anaerobe cannot tolerate oxygen and grows only where it is absent. A facultative anaerobe tolerates both conditions and can respire with or without oxygen. Growth without oxygen on its own does not show which category an organism belongs to.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can every organism switch to anaerobic respiration when oxygen runs out?
items.correct: No. Obligate aerobes require oxygen and cannot grow without it; only facultative anaerobes and obligate anaerobes can grow in the absence of oxygen.
items.misconception: All organisms can fall back on anaerobic respiration if oxygen is unavailable, so no organism strictly needs oxygen to survive.
items.why: The examples of anaerobic respiration that students meet first are human muscle during exercise and yeast in fermentation, both organisms that switch between modes, so switching is taken to be universal. Obligate aerobes are defined by their inability to tolerate the absence of oxygen: they can grow only in aerobic conditions. Yeast can grow with or without oxygen and is a facultative anaerobe. Humans, despite brief anaerobic respiration in muscle cells, cannot survive without oxygen gas in their environment and are obligate aerobes; the ability to switch modes at the organism level is not shared by all organisms.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a facultative anaerobe prefer conditions without oxygen?
items.correct: No. A facultative anaerobe uses oxygen for aerobic cell respiration whenever oxygen is available and switches to anaerobic respiration only when oxygen is absent.
items.misconception: A facultative anaerobe is basically an anaerobe: it lives by anaerobic respiration and merely tolerates oxygen without using it.
items.why: The noun in the name is 'anaerobe', so students take anaerobic respiration to be the organism's normal mode and 'facultative' to mean it can put up with oxygen. The word 'facultative' itself is unfamiliar. 'Facultative' means the organism has the option of either mode. Because aerobic cell respiration yields far more ATP per glucose, a facultative anaerobe respires aerobically when oxygen is present and grows better in those conditions; it respires anaerobically only when oxygen is absent.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do photosynthetic prokaryotes contain chloroplasts?
items.correct: No. Prokaryotic cells have no chloroplasts or other membrane-bound organelles; photosynthetic prokaryotes carry out photosynthesis using pigments and membranes within the cell.
items.misconception: Any organism that photosynthesizes must contain chloroplasts, so photosynthetic bacteria have chloroplasts.
items.why: Chloroplasts are taught as 'the site of photosynthesis', so students treat the organelle and the process as inseparable. Cell diagrams of photosynthetic organisms are almost always of plant cells. Chloroplasts are found in plant and algal cells. Prokaryotic cells lack all membrane-bound organelles, yet several groups of prokaryotes photosynthesize, which shows that the process does not require a chloroplast.
items.specStatementText: Photosynthesis feeds plants, algae and some prokaryotes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do plants obtain their food from the soil?
items.correct: No. Plants are autotrophs: they synthesize their own carbon compounds from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. They absorb only water and mineral ions from the soil.
items.misconception: Plants absorb their food from the soil through their roots, in the same way that animals take in food.
items.why: Fertilisers are sold as 'plant food', and the roots are the obvious 'mouth' of a plant, so students assume that the soil supplies the plant's food and that photosynthesis merely adds energy to it. Autotrophs make their own carbon compounds from inorganic substances. Mineral ions from the soil are needed in small amounts, but the carbon in a plant's sugars, starch, cellulose and proteins comes from carbon dioxide fixed in photosynthesis, not from the soil.
items.specStatementText: Photosynthesis feeds plants, algae and some prokaryotes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does digestion include the use of absorbed molecules to build new tissue?
items.correct: No. Digestion is the breakdown of ingested food into small molecules; building the organism's own molecules from those products is assimilation.
items.misconception: Digestion is everything that happens to food inside the body, including turning it into the animal's own tissues.
items.why: In everyday speech 'digesting' a meal means the whole of what the body does with it, so students extend the term to cover every stage after ingestion. Digestion is a specific stage of holozoic nutrition: the internal hydrolysis of large food molecules into small ones that can be absorbed. What happens to those molecules after absorption is assimilation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does ingestion mean in holozoic nutrition?
items.correct: Taking food into the body, for example through the mouth into the gut, before it is digested.
items.misconception: Ingestion is the uptake of food molecules into cells, so cells 'ingest' amino acids and glucose.
items.why: 'Ingest' is used loosely in everyday English for taking anything in, and students have met phagocytes 'engulfing' particles, so the term is applied to uptake at the cell level rather than to the whole organism taking in food. In holozoic nutrition, ingestion is the first stage: food is taken into the body, in animals usually through a mouth into a gut. Uptake of the products of digestion by cells is part of assimilation, the final stage.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does 'obligate' mean when applied to a mixotroph?
items.correct: An obligate mixotroph must use both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition; neither mode alone can sustain it. A facultative mixotroph can survive on one mode alone.
items.misconception: An obligate mixotroph is one that is obliged to photosynthesize; it only occasionally feeds heterotrophically, whereas a facultative mixotroph is free to do either.
items.why: Students have just met 'obligate aerobe', where 'obligate' attaches to one condition, and they carry the pattern over by attaching 'obligate' to the mode they think of as primary, photosynthesis, instead of to the combination. In 'obligate mixotroph' the word 'obligate' refers to mixotrophy itself: the organism must combine both modes to survive. In 'facultative mixotroph' the organism can live by one mode alone and uses the other when conditions favour it.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is mixotrophy a rare curiosity confined to freshwater protists such as Euglena?
items.correct: No. Euglena is the well-known freshwater example, but many mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton, where mixotrophy is widespread.
items.misconception: Mixotrophy is an oddity found in a few freshwater species, of which Euglena is essentially the only example.
items.why: Euglena is the single example in most textbooks and the only mixotroph students have seen under a microscope, so it stands in for the whole category. The guidance notes that many other mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton. Mixotrophy is a common mode of nutrition in the open ocean, not an exception.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are earthworms and woodlice saprotrophs?
items.correct: No. They ingest dead organic matter and digest it internally, so they are detritivores using holozoic nutrition. Saprotrophic nutrition is external digestion by fungi and bacteria, which the guide says can be referred to as decomposers.
items.misconception: Any organism that feeds on dead organic matter, including earthworms, woodlice and dung beetles, is a saprotroph.
items.why: GCSE uses 'decomposer' loosely for anything that breaks down dead material, and earthworms are the most visible organisms in leaf litter and compost. Saprotrophic nutrition is defined by external digestion followed by absorption. Animals that eat dead matter ingest it and digest it internally, so they are detritivores, not saprotrophs, whatever broader label is used for them.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are fungi autotrophic, like plants?
items.correct: No. Fungi are heterotrophs; many are saprotrophs that obtain carbon compounds from dead organic matter by external digestion.
items.misconception: Fungi are a type of plant and make their own carbon compounds, because they are rooted in place and do not move or eat.
items.why: Fungi were classified as plants until the twentieth century and are still grouped with plants in gardening and everyday speech; their immobility matches the student's mental image of an autotroph. Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesize. They are heterotrophic: saprotrophic fungi secrete enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorb the products, which is why they can be referred to as decomposers.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all archaea obtain energy in the same way?
items.correct: No. Archaea are metabolically very diverse: different species use light, the oxidation of inorganic chemicals, or the oxidation of carbon compounds to provide energy for ATP production.
items.misconception: All archaea are chemosynthetic extremophiles that get energy from inorganic chemicals in places such as hot springs and deep-sea vents.
items.why: Archaea are introduced through the striking examples of hot-spring and deep-sea vent organisms, so the whole domain is assumed to share that single lifestyle. The guidance stresses that archaea are metabolically very diverse. Some use light energy, some oxidize inorganic chemicals and some oxidize carbon compounds obtained from other organisms. Many archaea live in ordinary soils and oceans rather than in extreme environments.
items.specStatementText: Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all prokaryotes heterotrophic decomposers?
items.correct: No. Archaea are metabolically very diverse: different species obtain energy for ATP production from light, from the oxidation of inorganic chemicals, or from the oxidation of carbon compounds. Only the last of these depends on carbon compounds from other organisms.
items.misconception: All prokaryotes, including archaea, are heterotrophs that obtain energy by oxidizing carbon compounds from dead organic matter.
items.why: Bacteria are met at GCSE mainly as decomposers and pathogens, both of which are heterotrophs, so heterotrophy is assumed to be the prokaryotic way of life. The guidance states that archaea species use either light, oxidation of inorganic chemicals or oxidation of carbon compounds to provide energy for ATP production. Only the third of these routes takes its energy from carbon compounds obtained from other organisms; archaea that use light or inorganic chemicals as their energy source are not decomposers, so 'all prokaryotes are heterotrophic decomposers' is false.
items.specStatementText: Archaea: a domain of their own, metabolically diverse

items.q: Can the diet of an extinct hominid be deduced, or is it only guesswork?
items.correct: It can be deduced. Theories relating dentition to diet, developed from observations of living mammals, are applied to the fossil dentition to deduce the diet.
items.misconception: Statements about what an extinct species ate are speculation, because nobody was there to observe it feeding.
items.why: Students equate scientific knowledge with direct observation, so anything that cannot be watched seems to them to be a guess. The NOS idea that theories allow deductions about unobservable cases is unfamiliar. Deductions can be made from theories. Observation of living mammals established how dentition relates to herbivorous or carnivorous diets; applying that theory to a fossil skull gives a reasoned deduction about the extinct animal's diet, which can be tested against other evidence such as tooth wear.

items.q: Do plants have adaptations that resist herbivory?
items.correct: Yes. Plants resist herbivory with thorns and other physical structures, and by producing toxic secondary compounds in seeds and leaves.
items.misconception: Plants are passive food for herbivores; they cannot defend themselves and can only regrow after being eaten.
items.why: Plants do not move or react visibly, and students see grazing animals eating grass without difficulty, so plants are assumed to be defenceless. Plants are actively adapted against herbivores. Physical structures such as thorns, spines and tough leaves deter feeding, and many seeds and leaves contain toxic secondary compounds that poison or deter the animals that eat them.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do plants contain toxic secondary compounds in their leaves and seeds?
items.correct: They are adaptations for resisting herbivory: the compounds poison or deter animals that eat the plant, protecting the leaves and the seeds in particular.
items.misconception: Secondary compounds are metabolic waste products that the plant stores in its leaves because it cannot excrete them; any effect on herbivores is incidental.
items.why: Students learn that plants have no excretory system and that leaf fall removes waste, and an older 'waste product' explanation of secondary metabolites still appears in some sources. The guidance states that plants produce toxic secondary compounds in seeds and leaves as a means of resisting herbivory. Their concentration in the parts most valuable to the plant, such as seeds, reflects their role as a defence.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are plant secondary compounds harmful only to insects?
items.correct: No. Many secondary compounds are toxic to mammals and other vertebrates as well; herbivorous mammals that eat such plants need adaptations to cope with them.
items.misconception: Plant toxins deter insects but are harmless to mammals, because mammals such as cows and sheep eat plants without difficulty.
items.why: The herbivores students know best are livestock grazing grass, which is low in toxins, so plants are assumed to be safe food for any mammal. Toxic secondary compounds in seeds and leaves act against a wide range of herbivores. Mammals that specialise on toxic plants have metabolic adaptations for detoxifying them.

items.q: Why does an aphid pierce a leaf?
items.correct: To insert its stylets into the leaf and feed on sap; the piercing mouthparts are a feeding adaptation.
items.misconception: Aphids pierce leaves in order to inject a toxin that kills or digests the leaf tissue, as a mosquito or wasp injects a substance.
items.why: The only piercing insects most students know are mosquitoes and stinging wasps, so piercing is associated with injecting rather than with feeding. The piercing mouthparts of leaf-eating insects are an adaptation for feeding on plants: the stylets reach the sap inside the leaf so it can be drawn up and ingested.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a behaviour, such as living in a herd, be an adaptation?
items.correct: Yes. Behavioural adaptations are inherited patterns of behaviour that help predators catch prey or help prey resist predation.
items.misconception: Adaptations are anatomical features; behaviours are learned by the individual, so they do not count as adaptations.
items.why: Adaptation is introduced with structural examples such as beaks and fur, and students think of behaviour as something an animal decides to do rather than as a heritable trait. The guidance requires students to be aware of behavioural adaptations in both predators and prey, for example pack hunting, ambushing, herding, nocturnal activity and alarm calls. These have a genetic basis and are subject to natural selection like any other trait.

items.q: Is camouflage only an adaptation of prey animals?
items.correct: No. Camouflage is a physical adaptation of many predators too, allowing them to approach or ambush prey unseen.
items.misconception: Camouflage is a defence used by prey; predators have no need to hide.
items.why: Camouflage is taught with prey examples such as stick insects and peppered moths, and predators are pictured as bold and dominant. Adaptations for finding, catching and killing prey include physical adaptations such as the camouflaged coats of leopards and the patterns of ambush predators. The same feature can serve prey and predator in different species.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do epiphytes take nutrients from the trees they grow on?
items.correct: No. Epiphytes use the tree only as a support to reach light; they obtain water and minerals from rain and debris, and their carbon compounds come from their own photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Epiphytes are parasites that draw water and carbon compounds from the host tree's tissues.
items.why: A plant growing on another plant with no soil looks as though it must be feeding on its host, and mistletoe, a genuine parasite that grows on branches, is a familiar example. An epiphyte is a plant growing on the branches of a tree for support, not a parasite. Its strategy for harvesting light is to start high in the forest where light is available, and it photosynthesizes for itself.
items.specStatementText: Ways to reach the light in a forest

items.q: Are forest floor plants kept alive by sugar passed to them from canopy trees through fungal networks?
items.correct: No. Shade-tolerant herbs and shrubs make their own carbon compounds by photosynthesis at low light intensity; they are autotrophs.
items.misconception: Canopy trees feed the plants beneath them with sugar through an underground 'wood wide web' of fungi.
items.why: Popular books and documentaries on the 'wood wide web' present trees as nurturing the forest floor, and students generalise this to the nutrition of understory plants. The strategy of forest floor herbs and shrubs is shade tolerance: photosynthesis at low light intensities. Their carbon compounds are the product of their own photosynthesis, not a supply from canopy trees.

items.q: Is growing tall the only way a forest plant can obtain enough light?
items.correct: No. Forest plants use different strategies: trees reach the canopy, lianas climb, epiphytes grow on high branches, strangler epiphytes start high and root downwards, and shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs photosynthesize on the forest floor.
items.misconception: Every plant in a forest is racing to the canopy; those that stay low are losing the competition for light and will die.
items.why: Competition for light is presented as a race upwards, and 'survival of the fittest' language makes students expect a single winning strategy. The guidance lists several distinct strategies for reaching light in forests. Plants that do not reach the canopy are not failed trees: lianas, epiphytes and shade-tolerant herbs occupy different niches and are adapted to obtain light in different ways.

items.q: Which is larger, a species' fundamental niche or its realized niche?
items.correct: The fundamental niche. It is the potential niche set by adaptations and tolerance limits; the realized niche is the smaller part actually occupied when in competition with other species.
items.misconception: The fundamental niche is the range a species is actually found in, and the realized niche is the wider range it could potentially occupy.
items.why: In everyday English 'fundamental' means basic or core, which sounds like the observed reality, while 'realized' is read as 'could be realised', that is, potential. 'Realized' means actually brought about. The realized niche is the actual extent of the niche when in competition; the fundamental niche is the potential based on adaptations and tolerance limits, so the realized niche can never be larger than the fundamental niche.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a competitor is removed and a species spreads into new areas, has its tolerance changed?
items.correct: No. Its tolerance limits, and so its fundamental niche, are unchanged; the species has simply been able to occupy more of a fundamental niche it already had.
items.misconception: Removing a competitor causes the species to adapt so that it can tolerate the newly available conditions.
items.why: Students think of adaptation as something an organism does in response to circumstances during its life, and read a change in distribution as a change in the organism. The fundamental niche is the potential set by a species' existing adaptations and tolerance limits. A shift in distribution after a competitor is removed is a change in the realized niche, not evidence of new tolerance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does one species eliminate another through competition?
items.correct: By using a shared resource, such as food or space, more effectively, so that the other species cannot obtain enough to grow and reproduce; there is no direct attack.
items.misconception: The winning species eliminates the other by killing or eating it.
items.why: Elimination suggests violence, and predation is the interaction between species that students find most vivid, so competition is imagined as a fight. Competition is an interaction between species that need the same limited resource. Elimination happens because one species leaves too little of the resource for the other, not because it preys on it.
